narrative:
The model estimates a 59% chance that you will fail your final year. In practical terms, this is slightly more likely than not, so the school is treating you as needing remedial courses rather than waiting until the year end.

The strongest reason is your intention about higher education: you have said you do not want to continue to higher education, while every student who passed in the comparison group wanted to. That lack of a longer-term academic goal was the largest push toward a failing prediction. The next most important factor actually works in your favour: you have no past class failures, which is the same as the passed-group average and pushes the prediction toward passing. Still, it was not enough to offset the concerns. The third factor is your weekly study time: you report less than two hours, while most passed students study two to five hours, and only about one in five passed students study under two hours. This low study time pushes toward failing.

To improve your chances, treat the remedial courses as a chance to build a clearer goal: decide whether continuing education is worthwhile, and discuss this with your family or school counsellor. Increase weekly study time to at least two to five hours, ideally with a regular schedule, and use available family or school support. Keep your attendance steady and protect your record of no past failures.
